title: Reply Comments of Earthjustice in response to the stakeholder's comments re PJM Interconnection, LLC's 02/23/2026 Initial Brief et al. under EL25-49, et al.

documents.name: Reply Comments of Earthjustice.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION




    PJM Interconnection, LLC                                   )                   Docket No. EL25-49-000
                                                               )                 Docket No. ER26-1479-000
                                                               )

                                     Reply Comments of Earthjustice

    I.       Introduction

         On February 23, 2026, PJM Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”) submitted its initial brief1 and

60-day compliance filing2 in response to the Commission’s December 18, 2025, order on the

show cause proceeding.3 Earthjustice appreciates the opportunity to respond to the wide range of

comments that stakeholders submitted to the Commission in response to PJM’s filings.4 As PJM

and other commenters remark, PJM is tasked with reimagining how it will provide transmission

services, among other system changes. To date, PJM’s region has absorbed more load growth

from large load customers than any other grid operator in the Commission’s jurisdiction. And

projected load growth through 2030 is not slowing down.5




1
  Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49-000 (Feb. 23, 2026), Accession No. 20260223-
5189 (“PJM Initial Brief”).
2
  60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access Transmission Tariff to Comply
with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49, et. al, Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Feb. 23, 2026), Accession No.
20260223-5181 (“60-Day Compliance Filing”).
3
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order on Show Cause Proceeding”).
4
  These comments are timely filed in Docket No. EL25-49-000. Though PJM chose to file its 60-Day Compliance
Filing in a separate docket, ER26-1479-000, all of the issues discussed in these comments were initially raised in the
Commission’s Order on the Show Cause Proceeding in Docket No. EL25-49-000. We respectfully request that the
Commission consider these comments in both EL25-49-000 and ER26-1479-000.
5
  John Wilson, et. al., Power Demand Forecasts Revised Up for Third Year Running, Led by Data Centers, Grid
Strategies 5 (2025), https://gridstrategiesllc.com/wp-content/uploads/Grid-Strategies-National-Load-Growth-Report-
2025.pdf.

                                                          1
           With this landscape, PJM has little margin for error in implementing the new and

modified services to avoid events that could devastate system reliability. As explained below, to

avoid such risks, the Commission should (1) accept PJM’s proposed operational penalties;

(2) require PJM to clarify how and when curtailment directives will be enforced and how

violations will be communicated to the public; (3) decline to require that PJM rush the

implementation of protection mechanisms for its new non-firm transmission services; and

(4) require PJM to make its co-located generator interconnection studies and retail-BTMG rules

consistent with the Commission’s Order on the Show Cause Proceeding and Order No. 2023.

          Additionally, several comments in this docket express concern about PJM’s

interconnection queue, with commenters fearing delays.6 The Commission is aware of PJM’s

clogged interconnection queue and has raised concerns over PJM’s potential reliability and

resource adequacy issues.7 Other regulators have expressed similar concerns.8 This docket

reinforces that the Commission should require PJM to accelerate its interconnection process and

ensure consistency with open access.

    II.      The Commission should accept PJM’s operational penalty proposal.

          The Commission should accept PJM’s proposed operational penalties for data centers9

taking PJM’s new transmission services because financial penalties alone are insufficient to

1479-000 (Mar. 16, 2026), Accession No. 20260316-5300 (“AEU & SEIA Protest”); Protest of Joint Parties, at 7 n.
32, Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Mar. 16, 2026), Accession No. 20260316-5333 (“Joint Parties Protest”);
Comments of the Digital Power Network, at 5, Docket No. ER26-1479-000 (Mar. 16, 2026), Accession No.
20260316-5220.
7
  Order on Show Cause Proceeding, supra note 3, at P 243.
8
  Statement of Principles Regarding PJM (Jan. 16, 2026), https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-
regarding-pjm.
9
  PJM’s proposal will apply to “Eligible Customers,” which PJM defines as “(1) any electric utility or any person
generating electric energy for sale for resale, but with respect to transmission service that the Commission is
prohibited from ordering by section 212(h) of the Federal Power Act, such entity is eligible only if the service is
provided pursuant to a state requirement that the Transmission Provider or Transmission Owner offer the unbundled

                                                        2
 ensure compliance with curtailment directives. The Commission’s Order on the Show Cause

Proceeding directs PJM to brief and establish an appropriate penalty charge and “any other

remedial action” that PJM should take to address a customer’s unreserved use of the transmission

system or excess energy withdrawals.10 Pursuant to the Commission’s order, PJM establishes

three different penalties—pause in service, disqualification, and financial penalties—

applicable where data centers fail to follow Load Shedding and Curtailment directives, rely on

necessary control technologies that fail more than once, or make unreserved use of the

transmission system. While PJM and Transmission Owners (“TOs”) propose to assess additional

financial penalties for a customer’s unreserved use of the transmission system, PJM and TOs

correctly acknowledge that financial penalties alone are not enough to incentivize data centers to

follow curtailment procedures.11 Because financial penalties are insufficient to ensure that data

centers will curtail energy use, the Commission should accept PJM’s more rigorous operational

penalties.

        A. Initial comments either support PJM proposed penalties or fail to adequately
           address PJM’s argument that financial penalties are insufficient to ensure
           compliance.

        Commenters generally support penalties for data centers that fail to follow curtailment

procedures but disagree on whether PJM should impose its proposed operational penalties as

opposed to solely financial penalties. Commenters who have a responsibility to ensure reliability,




transmission service, or pursuant to a voluntary offer of such service by a Transmission Owner or (2) any retail
customer taking unbundled transmission service pursuant to a state requirement that the Transmission Provider or a
Transmission Owner offer the transmission service, or pursuant to a voluntary offer of such service by a
Transmission Owner.” PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart A, Section 400, Definitions E.
However, for simplicity, these comments refer to Eligible Customers as “data centers” because the majority of
Eligible Customers will be taking service on behalf of data center customers.
10
   Order on Show Cause Proceeding, supra note 3, at P 212, 217.
11
   PJM’s Initial Brief, supra note 1, at 50.

                                                         3
 including the Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative (“NOVEC”) and TOs, support PJM’s

operational penalties and emphasize PJM’s obligation to protect the transmission system.

NOVEC states that a pause in service and disqualification are appropriate and necessary to

reliably manage co-location arrangements and protect the integrity of PJM’s transmission

system.12 NOVEC also agrees that financial penalties alone are insufficient to ensure that data

centers comply with their curtailment obligations, though both NOVEC and TOs support

imposing complementary financial penalties alongside PJM’s proposed operational penalties.13

        Unsurprisingly, developers of co-located resources argue for a weaker penalty structure

based solely on financial penalties—but fail to show that financial penalties can actually affect

their behavior. Joint Co-location Developers suggest PJM use a financial penalty similar to the

Non-Performance Charge PJM assesses in the Capacity Resource context.14 They argue that

PJM’s operational penalties are disproportionate to the harm caused by data centers that fail to

curtail.15 They assert that “failure to respond to a Load Shedding or Curtailment procedure would

have a similar impact to a capacity resource failing to perform during emergency events,” while

the opportunity cost of shutting down a data center could purportedly be higher than the penalty

charge ordinarily levied on capacity resources for failing to curtail.16

        Joint Co-location Developers also argue that forcing a data center to take Network

Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) after a single unauthorized withdrawal is unfair and

will threaten the commercial viability of PJM’s proposal.17 Other commenters argue that PJM’s

Accession No. 20260325-5220 (“NOVEC Comments”).

EL25-49-000 (Mar. 25, 2026), Accession No. 20260325-5203 (“TOs Response Brief”).
14
   Reply Brief of Joint Co-Location Developers, at 25, Docket No. EL25-49-000 (Mar. 25, 2026), Accession No.
20260325-5236 (“Co-Location Developers Reply Brief”).
15

 strict liability rules unfairly assign penalties to load customers regardless of the cause or whether

a third party is at fault.18

        Commenters opposing operational penalties believe instead that financial penalties are

sufficient to deter wrongful conduct, although they provide no explanation of why this is

purportedly the case other than their references to other PJM penalties levied in different

contexts. As detailed below, comments opposing PJM’s proposed operational penalties are

unpersuasive because in addition to being self-serving, they ignore critical facts. Such comments

fail to explain how financial penalties alone could be effective. They also disregard how data

centers’ failure to curtail can pose extreme risks to reliability.

             1. PJM’s operational penalties are proportionate to the prospective harm
                 associated with a customer’s failure to follow curtailment orders.

         PJM explains that the consequences of a Remedial Action Scheme (“RAS”)

misoperation are more severe than failures of other fault protection schemes.19 A data center’s

RAS misoperation or failure to comply with curtailment directives could have dire consequences

for reliability, including the loss of all interim or non-firm load in one area—or even cascading

outages across the Eastern Interconnection.20 These serious consequences warrant serious

penalties. While opposing commenters note that PJM’s proposed penalties are stricter than the

penalties it has levied in other circumstances, those comments fail to acknowledge that the stakes

here are higher.

        As the Commission points out in its December 18 order, NERC has stated that “co-

location of large loads with generation facilities can have substantial reliability impacts due


18
   Id. at 25-26, Response of the Data Center Coalition, at 8, Docket No. EL25-49-000 (Mar. 25, 2026), Accession
No. 20260325-5208 (“DCC Comments”).
19
   PJM Initial Brief, supra note 1, at 43.
20
   PJM Initial Brief, Attach C., Affidavit of Matthew Wharton on behalf of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at P 21, 22
(“Wharton Affidavit”).

                                                         5
 to . . . loss of load incidents, while also presenting unique challenges and opportunities for grid

transformation that require special consideration.”21 The unique challenges and opportunities of

co-location arrangements require unique solutions. It is not enough to hope that financial

penalties used in other circumstances—which, as explained below, did not actually work—will

encourage data centers taking these new services to follow curtailment directives, especially

when the reliability risks here are greater. The Commission must ensure that the penalties for

failure to curtail are commensurate with the serious risks for PJM’s transmission system and

ultimately customers such as residential ratepayers.

           2. PJM’s obligation to offer non-firm service is not without limits.

           PJM’s proposal to require data centers to take NITS after failure to follow curtailment

orders is also reasonable. PJM’s new transmission services are explicitly designed for colocation

arrangements to connect faster in exchange for promises to curtail when directed. It is reasonable

to revoke a data center’s ability to use these new transmission services if a data center fails to

uphold its end of the bargain. Otherwise, data centers would receive the benefits of these

transmission services without providing a commensurate benefit to the grid. Simply put, large

loads that fail to curtail when instructed cannot be trusted not to repeat that failure, especially in

light of the severe reliability risks they present. While data centers that fail to curtail when

instructed may have to wait for network upgrades before they can take NITS, that outcome is an

entirely reasonable consequence for their failure to deliver promised flexibility.

           3. PJM’s penalty proposal is appropriately designed to protect system reliability, rather
           than assign fault.

           PJM’s proposal also reasonably addresses the concern that it may assign penalties to

large load customers no matter who is at fault. Where failure to curtail results from a mishap


21
     Order on Show Cause Proceeding, supra note 3, at P 136.

                                                         6
 with control technologies—for which a large load may not be at fault—PJM proposes a pause in

service to provide a chance to correct the problems. Throughout the subsequent evaluation

period, PJM and TOs will be able to investigate the issue and implement fixes, while also

allowing the data center to resume the service once the fixes are in place.22 This evaluation

period reasonably allows PJM to get to the root of the issue without disqualifying the load

customer.

        Some commenters speculate that other factors outside their control could cause a failure

to curtail, such as problems with TOs’ facilities or communication systems. Setting aside the

speculative nature of these concerns, PJM reasonably addresses this prospect by proposing an

implementation timeline that will allow PJM and TOs to develop sufficiently sophisticated

curtailment procedures. As PJM requires data centers to demonstrate their ability to fully comply

with Load Shedding and Curtailment Procedures before the Service Commencement Date to

begin service, PJM similarly must ensure that the systems that PJM and TOs will use to issue

load shedding and curtailment directives will be robust.

        The Commission should not allow hypothetical mishaps to prevent PJM from

implementing meaningful operational penalties. PJM has correctly described the seriousness of

misoperation and failures to curtail and has given itself a three-year timeline to implement its

curtailment scheme to ensure that the necessary modifications can be made for curtailment

procedures.23 PJM’s decision to approach this issue with adequate caution and care is reasonable

and will decrease the likelihood that the commenters’ hypothetical concerns will arise.




22
  PJM Initial Brief, supra note 1, at 44-45.
23
  PJM Initial Brief, Attach. D, Affidavit of Timothy Horger on behalf of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at P 16.
(“Horger Affidavit”).

                                                        7
          B. The Commission should accept PJM’s proposed penalties because financial
            penalties alone are insufficient to ensure that data centers will comply with
            curtailment directives.

         PJM is correct that financial penalties alone are not enough to incentivize data centers to

follow curtailment or load shed procedures. Some commenters have suggested that financial

penalties could in theory be sufficient to deter data centers from failing to curtail when

instructed,24 but no comments actually describe what financial penalty could be sufficient in

practice. That notable silence is likely because none of the commenters know what financial

penalty could convince large load customers—with virtually unlimited capital and very high

contractual uptime requirements—to curtail when directed. Though commenters argue that

operational penalties are too strict, they are far more effective than financial penalties. To be

effective, financial penalties must be more than merely the cost of doing business for well-

financed large loads. However, because data centers are wealthy and have diverse business

practices, calculating an effective financial penalty is extremely difficult. Moreover, payments

made after the fact will not prevent the harm from non-performance.

         Data center spending is growing exponentially, making it increasingly difficult to

determine a uniform financial rate that could convince this multi-billion dollar—soon trillion

dollar—industry to follow curtailment procedures instead of just paying the penalties. As of

December 2025, data center deals hit a new record of $61 billion globally.25 According to

McKinsey, global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030.26 With data center

investors.html.

telecommunications/our-insights/the-7-trillion-dollar-data-center-build-out-how-industrials-can-capture-their-share.

                                                         8
 spending increasing by billions year over year, it is impossible to gauge what level of financial

penalty could incentivize data centers to curtail their operations rather than just taking the

penalty charge as an operating cost. Indeed, new research suggests that there is no price level

currently observed in wholesale markets where certain data center loads will curtail.27

        Data centers’ low participation in demand response programs also indicates that financial

penalties are unlikely to be effective. In a study examining the potential for data center

flexibility, the Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability found that data

centers have historically had low participation rates in demand response programs, likely as a

result of their operational priorities and low financial incentives.28 Data centers are designed to

provide uninterrupted service, often with mandated benchmarks, including uptime, latency, and

quality of service.29 Responses to financial incentives, whether demand response payments or

financial penalties, could vary based on a data center’s particular operational capabilities. Data

centers are organized by tiers, ranging from tier I to tier IV.30 At the most basic capacity, tier I

offers 99.671% of uptime per year, leaving less than 28.8 hours of downtime per year, and tier

IV offers 99.995% of uptime per year, leaving less than 26.3 minutes of downtime per

year.31 For large loads with “high utilization rates and controlling costs, the economic

data-center-tiers-classifications.

                                                         9
 proposition of demand response participation may be unattractive.”32 Just as demand response

payments are insufficient to entice flexibility, financial penalties will be insufficient to compel

flexibility.

         Although some data centers may be more likely to respond to financial incentives, the

diversity among data centers makes a uniform financial penalty impossible to calculate. Some

data centers have different operational priorities that could allow for more flexibility in their

energy usage33 Data centers used for artificial intelligence (“AI”) training purposes may be better

suited for flexible operations because they are able to defer their training operations, whereas

conventional data centers have less flexible real-time processing demands.34 For data centers

training AI, financial penalties could theoretically be more meaningful. But without knowing a

data center’s operating structure, service agreements, and priorities, there is no clear way to

figure out what level of financial penalty would be enough to incentivize a data center to curtail.

Additionally, many predict that in the longer term, AI training data centers will become less

important as AI models improve, and most data centers will ultimately be used for inference and

other, less flexible real-time processing applications. According to research by McKinsey, “by

2030 inference will surpass training to become the dominant workload in AI Data centers.”35

This trend further calls into question the long-term viability of data center load flexibility.

Additionally, some large-scale co-located data centers, like some at issue in this docket, house

multiple tenants, each with different operational requirements.36 A uniform financial penalty

33

35

telecommunications/our-insights/the-next-big-shifts-in-ai-workloads-and-hyperscaler-strategies
36

                                                     10
 alone would not be effective applied across all these different types of service arrangements,

which all have different operational and financial priorities.

        Indeed, PJM has used financial penalties in other contexts, and PJM is learning from its

mistakes. Joint Co-Location Developers attempt to compare underperforming capacity resources

to the data centers here, arguing that a rate similar to PJM’s Non-Performance Charge for a

capacity resource that fails to perform during an emergency would be appropriate and sufficient

in this context.37 However, PJM’s penalty charges for poorly performing capacity resources are

not a model for a penalty for large loads that abuse new transmission services for three key

reasons: (1) PJM’s Capacity Performance structure is ineffective; (2) PJM’s Capacity

Performance structure is designed to transfer penalties from underperforming resources to bonus

payments for overperforming resources, and there is no comparable structure for the new

transmission services; and (3) the risks of nonperformance for PJM’s curtailment procedures are

much graver than underperformance of a capacity resource during an emergency event.

        First, PJM’s Capacity Performance structure is ineffective. PJM implemented its

Capacity Performance system in response to capacity resource failures during the 2014 Polar

Vortex. The Polar Vortex hit the PJM region in January 2014, setting a record wintertime peak

demand.38 Twenty-two percent of PJM’s generation capacity failed to perform during the

storm.39 PJM attempted to address these nonperformance issues by creating a new Capacity

Performance system to incentivize capacity resources to perform during emergencies. PJM’s

Capacity Performance system assesses penalties, or Non-Performance Charges, to resources that

38

(May 8, 2014) (“Polar Vortex Report”), https://www.hydro.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/PJM-January-2014-
report.pdf.
39

                                                     11
 underperform during emergencies.40 PJM then uses those penalties to fund bonuses to resources

that overperformed during the emergency.41

        Unfortunately, PJM’s financial penalty system has not been an effective mechanism to

ensure that capacity resources perform when called. PJM created the Capacity Performance

system because it anticipated that emergency events like the Polar Vortex would occur again.

And PJM was right. But when an event like the Polar Vortex happened again, the Capacity

Performance system failed to incentivize resources to perform. Winter Storm Elliot hit the PJM

region in 2022 and despite PJM’s new penalty structure, PJM saw even more capacity resources

fail to perform in Winter Storm Elliott than in the Polar Vortex.42 These capacity resource

failures resulted in the largest Capacity Performance penalties that PJM has ever assessed, with

PJM charging underperforming resources $1.80 billion in Non-Performance Charges.43

However, in response to calls from generators to reduce the penalties, PJM has limited the

definition of an “Emergency Action” that would trigger penalties, which reduces instances where

PJM would assess penalties to nonperforming generators.44 PJM also entered into settlements to

reduce the penalties that PJM assessed to generators that failed to perform during Winter Storm

Elliott.45 Additionally, in 2022, the Commission confirmed that generators can include the risk of

increased Capacity Performance penalties in their market bids.46 This history—in which

 Capacity Performance penalties failed to compel strong performance from generators during

Winter Storm Elliott and were then watered down—makes clear that financial penalties are

insufficient to ensure performance in the Capacity Resource context. These financial penalties

would likely be even more inadequate to ensure that extremely wealthy data centers will curtail

as directed, where PJM has already acknowledged that data centers would likely “absorb

financial penalties” rather than follow curtailment procedures.47

         Second, even if financial penalties were effective in the Capacity Performance context,

PJM’s Capacity Performance structure is not comparable to a penalty system for new

transmission services. To start, the Capacity Performance system is designed to provide a

resettlement of the capacity market by charging penalties to underperforming resources that fund

bonus payments to overperforming resources. No similar resettlement approach is possible in the

context of these new transmission services, because there is no set of “overperforming” loads

that could ameliorate the harms from large loads that violate the terms of the new transmission

products. In this context, the only way to reduce the harm caused by failures to curtail is to stop

service to the large loads that violate the terms.

         Finally, large loads that violate the terms of new transmission products are not

comparable to underperforming generators because they pose far graver risks to reliability. PJM

explains that there could be dire loss of load events if all interim or non-firm loads in an

electrically close area have curtailment violations.48 If multiple customers in a close area have

similar RAS violations, the loss of one facility could require reducing or dropping all interim or

non-firm load in the area.49 Even worse, the failure or misoperation of one RAS in PJM could



47
   PJM Initial Brief, supra note 1, at 50.
48
   Wharton Affidavit, supra note 20, at P 22.
49
   Id.

                                                     13
 lead to cascading outages, which could affect the entire Eastern Interconnection.50 In contrast,

generator underperformance has not historically caused such severe harm. While the Polar

Vortex and Winter Storm Elliott featured generator failures and subsequent penalty charges, the

storms never caused widespread system outages.51 In contrast, the stakes are much higher for

PJM if customers taking its new transmission services fail to follow curtailment directives, and

PJM cannot risk its entire system to appease one category of customers. The Commission must

ensure that PJM is prioritizing reliability over the commercial interests of large loads. The

Commission should accept PJM’s operational penalty structure because financial incentives are

insufficient to incentivize performance or ensure reliability.

       III.      The Commission should require PJM to clarify how and when PJM will enforce
                 its curtailment procedures.

              While PJM’s proposed curtailment procedures and penalty structure are generally

reasonable, PJM has not provided sufficient detail about implementation. As failures to curtail

can cause dire ramifications for the transmission system, the Commission must have clarity on

several important points: (1) how PJM will communicate its curtailment directives to

Transmission Providers and Data centers; (2) how and when Transmission Providers will

determine that load shed is necessary, which loads will be curtailed first, and at what stage

curtailments will occur; and (3) how a data center will be disqualified and the timeline for that

disqualification.

              Additionally, the Commission should require PJM to explain how the public can obtain

records of violations of curtailment procedures and records of enforcement of penalties for those

violations. PJM has emphasized that misoperation of control technology and failures to respond


50
     Id.
51
     Winter Storm Elliott Report, supra note 42, at 1; Polar Vortex Report, supra note 38, at 1.

                                                            14
 to curtailment instructions can be detrimental to the transmission system, endanger reliability

across multiple regions, and even threaten the entire Eastern Interconnection. These reliability

risks mean that curtailment violations could significantly affect all of PJM’s ratepayers. With

stakes this high, the public must have access to information about how these risks and violations

play out.

     A. Initial comments urge the Commission to require PJM to clarify its proposed
        curtailment procedures.

        Initial comments explain that PJM’s initial brief did not provide sufficient detail about its

curtailment procedures. Several commenters argue that PJM did not provide adequate clarity

about key points, including (1) what specific conditions will trigger curtailments, (2) what the

earliest point is at which a Non-Firm customer can be curtailed and how far in advance

curtailment information will be provided, and (3) what the expected duration or frequency of

curtailment events is.52 Joint Co-Location Developers also seek clarification as to how PJM will

determine curtailment priority among its different classes of Non-Firm Service.53 Additionally,

Advanced Energy United (“AEU”) and the Solar Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”)

provide PJM with specific action items, requesting that PJM publish historical analysis and

forward-looking modeling of curtailment frequency and duration for the new Non-Firm

transmission services and hold a presentation to walk stakeholders through the curtailment

process.54 To address confusion around PJM’s curtailment procedures, the Commission should

require PJM to provide more information about specific curtailment triggers, curtailment

duration and frequency, and how the curtailment process will actually work.

        B. The Commission should require PJM to clarify its curtailment procedures to ensure
          that PJM will adequately protect the reliability and safety of the transmission
          system.

           In addition to the concerns raised in initial comments, PJM’s initial brief, tariff, and

proposed service agreements fail to adequately state (1) how PJM and its Transmission Providers

will direct customers to curtail, (2) how and when Transmission Providers will decide that load

shed is necessary and how they will choose which specific loads are curtailed first, (3) exactly

how and when disqualification will occur, and (4) how PJM will communicate curtailment

violations and disqualifications to the public. Without clarity on the issues, the Commission and

the public cannot be sure that PJM’s proposal can adequately protect the transmission system.

           PJM fails to state how it will actually communicate its orders to the Transmission

Providers and how the Transmission Providers will actually direct their customers to curtail.

PJM’s initial brief states that PJM will issue a directive to curtail, and data centers must

implement that directive and respond to any real-time instruction to curtail within five minutes.55

PJM’s proposed tariff further establishes that “the Transmission Provider will notify the data

center of any Curtailment in a timely manner” and that any requests to curtail will be consistent

with Good Utility Practice.56 Beyond that, PJM’s filings are silent as to how these directives will

be made known to data centers and what those directives will say. The Commission should

require PJM to clarify what the content of these directives will be and how these directives will

be communicated to data centers.

shed is necessary, how Transmission Providers will select specific loads to curtail, and at what

automatically applies after one instance of a data center failing to follow a curtailment directive

the data centers will stop receiving service or how PJM and Transmission Providers will disable

            Finally, the Commission should require PJM to explain how it will provide the public

with records of curtailment violations and subsequent disqualification. PJM is on the right track

to ensure that data centers comply with curtailment procedures. However, without proper

enforcement mechanisms and public transparency, regulators and the public will not be able to

evaluate the scope of risks to reliability and the efficacy of PJM’s penalty scheme. PJM has

described in detail how misoperations and failures to curtail can threaten the reliability of its

entire transmission system. The Commission should require PJM to post violations publicly,

ensuring that non-data center customers are aware of reliability threats and that violations are

handled appropriately.

IV.        The Commission should decline to require that PJM rush the implementation of
           protection mechanisms for its new non-firm transmission services.

           The Commission should approve PJM’s requested timeline to implement new

transmission services and accompanying RAS and Special Protection Schemes (SPS). Though

there is a strong push from some commenters to rush this process, the Commission must ensure

that PJM does not sacrifice the reliability of the transmission system to fulfill data centers’ near-

term power demands. The Commission has already expressed concern about the reliability and

resource adequacy implications of Co-Location Arrangements, stating in its December order that

“the speed at which co-located load can be added to the grid may pose particular resource

adequacy challenges, especially if co-location arrangements are not adequately and transparently

reflected in existing RA planning mechanisms.”63 Similarly, PJM has acknowledged that its new

transmission services and protection schemes could threaten the reliability of the transmission

system. Considering the serious threats to reliability, PJM must ensure that its systems are safe

 and reliable for all customers. The Commission and PJM must not rush the process to serve

certain customers at the expense of overall reliability.

        Commenters who have a responsibility to ensure reliability support PJM’s proposed

implementation date. PJM’s Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) and NOVEC both agree with

Mr. Horger’s explanation that the three-year timeline is necessary to give PJM enough time to

implement the modifications needed to support PJM’s new transmission services and curtailment

procedures.64 Similarly, NOVEC finds Mr. Horger’s explanation that it is no longer possible to

implement necessary changes to the 2028/2029 RPM to be well-founded and persuasive.65

Predictably, comments criticizing PJM’s deadline overwhelmingly come from entities with a

direct financial interest in developing co-located resources. These commenters push for urgency

and speed, calling for the Commission to require PJM to push up its deadline.

        The Commission should find that PJM’s deadline is appropriate for the planning and

training needed to implement PJM’s transmission services and curtailment protocols. PJM must

take appropriate time to implement new services and RAS. Getting it right is more important

than moving fast. Mr. Wharton’s affidavit acknowledges that the new transmission services and

its RAS and SPS schemes pose significant reliability risks.66 To limit reliability risks, PJM will

need to develop telemetry requirements for Co-Located Loads and ensure that necessary control

technologies and protective systems are properly designed.67 Typically, a RAS monitors one

specific, pre-determined condition, but those typical RASs would not be suitable here as PJM

will need an RAS or multiple RASs to monitor and activate for multiple conditions.68 As PJM

V.         The Commission should require PJM to ensure that rules governing generator
           interconnection studies and behind-the-meter generation are consistent with the
           Commission’s Order on the Show Cause Proceeding and Order No. 2023.

            PJM’s proposed rules are unjust and unreasonable because PJM’s proposed generator

interconnection study and behind-the-meter generation (“BTMG”) rules fail to comply with the

Commission’s Order on the Show Cause Proceeding and Order No. 2023. To ensure that PJM’s

rules are consistent with the Commission’s Orders, the Commission should: (1) require PJM to

clarify that hybrid resources can nominate their net withdrawal limitations for purposes of the

interconnection study process and (2) require PJM to set a materiality threshold for the amount

of load a generator can net using BTMG.

           The Commission ordered PJM to amend its tariff because it did not include conditions of

service for co-location arrangements that are willing and able to limit their withdrawals from the

transmission system. Despite the Commission’s orders, PJM’s proposed tariff is silent as to

whether a hybrid co-located facility can nominate net withdrawals for the purposes of PJM’s

 Necessary Study Process. Without incorporating the net withdrawal limitations of hybrid

generators in the operating assumptions for the Necessary Study Process, PJM’s proposed rules

will likely force hybrid generators to pay for unnecessary upgrades because the Necessary Study

Process will not accurately reflect hybrid generators’ use of the transmission system. The

Commission should require PJM to clarify that hybrid co-located facilities can nominate their net

withdrawal limitations for purposes of the Necessary Study Process to avoid excessive and

unnecessary network upgrade costs for hybrid generators.

       In addition to the Commission’s order to clarify the terms of service for co-location

arrangements, the Commission also ordered PJM to amend its retail-BTMG rules. The

Commission determined that PJM’s existing BTMG rules may lead to reliability and resource

adequacy risk and ordered PJM to create a MW materiality threshold for the amount of load a

Network Customer may net using BTMG. However, PJM proposes a Retail BTMG rule that is

fundamentally different from what the Commission ordered, limiting the size of generator that

can participate in BTMG netting instead of the amount of load that a generator may net. The

Commission should reject PJM’s materiality threshold and require PJM to make its retail-BTMG

rules consistent with the Commission’s Order on the Show Cause Proceeding.

   A. Initial Comments correctly urge the Commission to require PJM to clarify that
      hybrid resources can nominate net withdrawal limitations in PJM’s necessary study
      process.

       As initial comments explain, the Commission should require PJM to clarify that hybrid

resources may nominate net withdrawal limitations in PJM’s Necessary Study Process to avoid

triggering costly and unnecessary network upgrades. Joint Parties argue that without clear

provisions to allow hybrid generators to nominate net withdrawal limitations, PJM may include

 inaccurate operating assumptions for hybrid generators in its Necessary Study Process.70 These

assumptions could inaccurately identify overlapping grid impacts where storage resources and

co-located loads could instead manage withdrawals, triggering unnecessary network upgrades.71

If PJM fails to clarify that hybrid customers can nominate their net withdrawal limits, hybrid

generators may be forced to pay for and wait for network upgrades that they will not use.

        The Commission should require PJM to clarify that hybrid co-located facilities can

nominate their net withdrawal limitations for the necessary study process. This clarification

would be consistent not only with the Commission’s Order on its Show Cause Proceeding, but

also consistent with the Commission’s Order No. 2023. In Order No. 2023, the Commission

required transmission providers to use operating assumptions that reflect the proposed charging

behavior of storage resources, including hybrid facilities, in their interconnection studies.72 The

Commission issued these reforms to ensure that transmission providers do not overestimate the

impact of storage resources on the transmission system and to ensure that transmission providers

avoid assigning excessive and unnecessary network upgrades.73 PJM’s current proposal would be

inconsistent with Order No. 2023 by including inaccurate, overestimated assumptions in its

necessary study process for hybrid co-located resources. PJM’s proposal will likely trigger the

same excessive, unnecessary network upgrades that the Commission sought to prevent with

Order No. 2023. PJM must clarify that hybrid resources can nominate net withdrawal limitations

to comply with both the Commission’s Order on the Show Causing Proceeding and Order No.

2023.

      B. Initial comments correctly support revising PJM’s Retail-BTMG rules to be
        consistent with the Commission’s Order on the Show Cause Proceeding.

        Initial comments also urge the Commission to require PJM to change its proposed BTMG

rules because PJM’s proposal is unjust and unreasonable. PJM’s BTMG rules allow loads to

reduce their costs by netting their output from BTMG to determine their transmission charges.74

PJM’s proposed threshold limits retail-BTMG to generation that has a cumulative nameplate

rating of no greater than 50 MW.75 PJM’s proposed threshold is materially different from the

threshold that FERC ordered because PJM set a MW threshold for the size of generator that can

participate in netting rather than a threshold for the amount of load a generator can net.

Generators argue that PJM’s nameplate capacity cap unnecessarily limits the types of generators

that can participate in BTMG netting.76 Resources that would be excluded under PJM‘s current

proposal are technically capable of providing retail-BTMG and should be able to do so.77 Unlike

PJM’s proposed nameplate capacity threshold, the Commission’s load netting threshold would

apply fairly across all resource types. The Commission should reject PJM’s proposed BTMG

rules and require PJM to set a materiality threshold that is consistent with the Commission’s

Order on the Show Cause Proceeding.
